A 43-year-old man comes to the clinic with upper back pain that began 4 days ago after swimming. He
describes the pain as achy, rated 6/10, and worsened by movement. The pain radiates when he uses
his upper back muscles. He has no significant medical history and is not taking any medications. On
physical exam, the thoracic paraspinal muscles are bilaterally hypertonic and tender to palpation.
Motion testing reveals that the T2–T7 segments translate more easily to the right, while the cervical
and lumbar spine show relatively symmetric movement. To treat this patient using the facilitated
positional release (FPR) technique, what is the most appropriate next step? Answer Choices: (A)
Assess the tissues for dysfunction (B) Flatten the kyphotic curve from T1–T12 (C) Move T2–T7 into left
sidebending (D) Position T2–T7 into right rotation and right sidebending (E) Engage the restrictive
barrier of T2–T7 with direct pressure (F) Use indirect myofascial release to relax the thoracic paraspinal
muscles (G) Place the thoracic spine into flexion to exaggerate the kyphotic curve (H) Apply traction to
the thoracic spine while sidebending left (I) Rotate T2–T7 to the left while maintaining extension (J)
Shorten the paraspinal muscles on the right from T2–T7
 A. Assess the tissues for dysfunction
B. Rotate T2–T7 to the left while maintaining extension
C. Shorten the paraspinal muscles on the right from T2–T7
D. Position T2–T7 into right rotation and right sidebending
E. Place the thoracic spine into flexion to exaggerate the kyphotic curve
F. Flatten the kyphotic curve from T1–T12
G. Engage the restrictive barrier of T2–T7 with direct pressure
H. Apply traction to the thoracic spine while sidebending left
I. Move T2–T7 into left sidebending
J. Use indirect myofascial release to relax the thoracic paraspinal muscles
